evidence.label: Bloch’s conjecture for surfaces with p_g=0

headline: On a complex surface with no holomorphic two-forms, zero-cycles carry only their degree and Albanese data.
scope: It covers smooth connected projective complex surfaces with p_g = 0, with whole-number coefficients.
plain: A zero-cycle is a formal sum of points with whole-number coefficients. Bloch predicted that on surfaces with no holomorphic two-forms, very little information survives in such sums. Surfaces that are not of general type were handled in 1976. This paper claims to prove the remaining general-type case. No computer has checked the proof.
doesNot: This does not say anything about surfaces that carry a nonzero holomorphic two-form.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Bloch, Kas and Lieberman, non-general-type surfaces
scorecard.significanceWhy: If the proof holds, it settles a well-known conjecture on algebraic cycles that has been open for about 50 years.

explanation:
Mark three points a, b and c on a flat plane, extended to include its points at infinity. Write the bookkeeping sum 3a − 2b + c. Such a formal sum of points, with whole-number coefficients, is called a zero-cycle. Its degree is the sum of the coefficients, here 3 − 2 + 1 = 2. On this plane, the degree is all that matters. Any two points lie on a line. Along a line, one point can be slid to the other by an allowed move, called rational equivalence. So 3a − 2b + c is equivalent to 2 times any single point.

The rule comes from curves. On a curve inside the surface, a ratio of polynomials has zeros and poles. The zeros minus the poles count as a cycle equivalent to nothing. The Chow group of zero-cycles collects all zero-cycles, up to these moves[1]. The question is how much of this group survives beyond the degree.

The answer depends on special forms on the surface. A holomorphic two-form is a smooth complex way to measure small areas on the surface. Their count is written p_g. Mumford showed in 1969 that one such form makes the zero-cycles uncontrollably large[4]. They then admit no description by finitely many parameters. A second number, q, counts holomorphic one-forms. These give the Albanese variety, a torus that records what a zero-cycle of degree 0 can still detect. The map from zero-cycles of degree 0 to this torus is the Albanese map.

Bloch's conjecture predicts the converse of Mumford's result. If p_g is 0, the degree and the Albanese map should account for every zero-cycle[2]. When q is also 0, the torus is a single point. Then any two points of the surface should be equivalent[3]. In 1976, Bloch, Kas and Lieberman proved this for every surface that is not of general type[5]. Surfaces of general type are the most twisted class. So the open problem was general-type surfaces with p_g = q = 0[6].

These surfaces are rare and hard to build. For a minimal surface of general type with p_g = q = 0, one has b₂ = 10 − K²[15]. Here b₂ counts independent two-dimensional loops, and K² is a number between 1 and 9 attached to the surface. A Godeaux surface has K² = 1, so b₂ = 9. A surface with K² = 9 has b₂ = 1, like the plane. Earlier proofs needed extra structure on the surface, such as symmetries or quotient pictures[7]. Voisin handled Catanese and Barlow surfaces in 2014 through families of surfaces. Each method covered only some constructions.

This paper claims to prove Bloch's conjecture for every smooth projective complex surface with p_g = 0[9]. It treats p_g = q = 0 with no assumption on how the surface was built[10]. The remaining surfaces come from Bloch, Kas and Lieberman[11]. The argument needs no special family, cover or symmetry of the surface[8]. When p_g = q = 0, the paper also claims a consequence for powers of the surface. Every rational class on them is fixed by its cohomology class[16].

The obstacle is that loops and forms do not see rational equivalence. For these surfaces, all the loop data is algebraic. Even so, identities in cohomology do not settle rational equivalence by themselves[12]. The paper builds a relation among cycles on two copies of the surface. In it, the diagonal appears with a nonzero coefficient. The diagonal acts as the identity on zero-cycles, while the other terms kill zero-cycles of degree 0[14]. So degree-0 zero-cycles vanish, after allowing fractions. A known torsion theorem then removes the fractions. The relation comes from counting quotients of line bundles on the surface, with weights from a torus symmetry.

Recent preprints by Guletskii and Banerjee also propose proofs with overlapping scope[13]. The paper cites them as proposed proofs and uses a different method.

How sure is this? No Lean formalization is listed for this result. The proof rests on long calculations in enumerative geometry that no computer has checked. No specialist review has been published.
hypeCheck: No Lean check is listed. Other recent preprints propose proofs too, and no specialist review of any of them is published.

glossary.meaning: A formal sum of points on a shape, with whole-number coefficients.
The allowed moves on zero-cycles, coming from zeros and poles of functions on curves.
All zero-cycles up to rational equivalence.
A smooth complex way to measure small areas on a surface; their count is p_g.
A torus built from the holomorphic one-forms, which records what degree-0 zero-cycles can detect.
A member of the most twisted class of complex surfaces.
The sum of the coefficients of a zero-cycle.
